title: Open Question: Formalizing the Multinomial Distribution from the Multinomial Theorem
content: The header poses the open question inherited from `binomial-theorem-oq-02`: can the multinomial distribution and its moment-generating function be formalized purely from the multinomial theorem? The file answers YES by exhibiting the PMF, its normalization, and the MGF as three readings of the single Mathlib lemma `Finset.sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag`. The four imports are deliberately minimal — only the multinomial-coefficient and big-operators machinery — underscoring that no measure-theoretic apparatus is needed for the algebraic core.
mathContext: The multinomial distribution models $n$ independent trials each landing in one of the categories $i \in s$ with probability $p_i$ (where $\sum_{i \in s} p_i = 1$). The joint law of the category counts $(X_i)_{i \in s}$ is $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}\prod_{i \in s} p_i^{k_i}$ supported on $\{k : \sum_i k_i = n\}$. Its MGF is $M(t) = \bigl(\sum_{i\in s} p_i e^{t_i}\bigr)^n$. Both are specializations of $(\sum_i x_i)^n = \sum_{k} \binom{n}{k}\prod_i x_i^{k_i}$, the identity Mathlib packages as `sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag`.

title: multinomialProb: PMF Definition and Nonnegativity
content: `multinomialProb s p n k` defines the probability mass function of the multinomial distribution: $\binom{n}{k} \prod_{i \in s} p(i)^{k(i)}$ where $\binom{n}{k} = \text{Nat.multinomial}\, s\, k$ is the multinomial coefficient. The function is parameterized by a finite set $s$, probability function $p : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, number of trials $n$, and outcome function $k : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. `multinomialProb_nonneg` proves nonnegativity when all $p(i) \geq 0$ via `mul_nonneg`: the multinomial coefficient casts to $\geq 0$, and the product of powers of nonneg numbers is nonneg.
mathContext: The multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k_1,\ldots,k_m} = \frac{n!}{k_1! \cdots k_m!}$ counts the number of ways to assign $n$ distinguishable trials to $m$ outcome categories with $k_i$ trials in category $i$. In Lean, `Nat.multinomial s k` with `∑ i ∈ s, k i = n` gives this coefficient. The `piAntidiag s n` finset contains exactly the functions $k : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ with support in $s$ and $\sum k(i) = n$ — the valid outcome distributions.

title: multinomialProb_sum_eq_one: Normalization IS the Multinomial Theorem
content: `multinomialProb_sum_eq_one` proves $\sum_{k : \sum k = n} P(k) = 1$ in 3 lines: unfold the definition, apply `Finset.sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` (the multinomial theorem), then rewrite using $\sum p(i) = 1$ to get $1^n = 1$. The proof is: `rw [hp, one_pow] at h; exact h.symm`. The multinomial theorem literally *is* the normalization proof — no further work needed.
mathContext: The multinomial theorem states $(\sum_{i \in s} x_i)^n = \sum_{k \in \text{piAntidiag}\, s\, n} \binom{n}{k} \prod_{i \in s} x_i^{k(i)}$. Setting $x_i = p(i)$ and using $\sum p(i) = 1$: the left side becomes $1^n = 1$. The right side is $\sum_{k} \text{multinomialProb}\, s\, p\, n\, k$. This identifies probability normalization with the multinomial theorem, showing probability theory and combinatorics are two faces of the same algebraic identity.

title: MGF Derivation: multinomial_weighted_sum and multinomial_mgf_factored
content: `multinomial_weighted_sum` proves $(\sum p(i) \cdot g(i))^n = \sum_{k} \binom{n}{k} \prod (p(i) g(i))^{k(i)}$ — again a direct application of `sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` with $f(i) = p(i) \cdot g(i)$. `multinomial_mgf_factored` then factors $(p(i) g(i))^{k(i)} = p(i)^{k(i)} \cdot g(i)^{k(i)}$ using `Finset.prod_mul_distrib` and `mul_pow`, separating probability weights from the $g$-terms. This works over *any commutative semiring* — not just $\mathbb{R}$.
mathContext: The generality is key: the MGF derivation holds in any `CommSemiring`, so it applies to formal power series (generating functions), polynomial rings, and more. The factorization $\prod (p \cdot g)^k = (\prod p^k)(\prod g^k)$ is the multiplicativity of the product over independent factors, proved by `Finset.prod_mul_distrib`. When $g(i) = \exp(t_i)$: $\sum P(k) \prod g(i)^{k(i)} = \mathbb{E}[\exp(\sum t_i X_i)] = (\sum p(i) e^{t_i})^n$, the classical MGF formula.

title: Specialization to ℝ and the Uniform Distribution
content: `multinomial_mgf_real` (lines 126–131) re-expresses the `CommSemiring` MGF identity over $\mathbb{R}$ so that the coefficient $\binom{n}{k}\prod p_i^{k_i}$ is literally `multinomialProb s p n k` — the proof closes with `rfl`, confirming the abstract and probabilistic forms are definitionally equal. `multinomialProb_uniform_sum` (lines 136–141) then instantiates normalization at the uniform law $p_i = 1/k$ over `Fin k`: the hypothesis $\sum_i p_i = 1$ reduces to $k \cdot \tfrac1k = 1$, discharged by `field_simp` after `Finset.card_fin`.
mathContext: The uniform multinomial corresponds to rolling a fair $k$-sided die $n$ times: every category has probability $1/k$, so $\sum_{i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k} \tfrac1k = k\cdot\tfrac1k = 1$ and normalization follows from `multinomialProb_sum_eq_one`. The positivity hypothesis $0 < k$ is needed so that $1/k$ is well defined and the cardinality cancels. This is the discrete-uniform base case from which entropy and typical-set arguments in information theory are built.

title: Binomial as 2-Outcome Multinomial: Bool-Indexed Distribution
content: `multinomial_is_binomial` proves that the multinomial distribution over `{false, true}` with $p(\text{true}) = p$, $p(\text{false}) = 1-p$ normalizes to 1. The proof calls `multinomialProb_sum_eq_one` after reducing $\sum_{b \in \{F,T\}} p(b) = (1-p) + p = 1$ via `ring`. `binomial_normalization` proves the same result directly: $((1-p) + p)^n = 1^n = 1$ by `simp`.
mathContext: For $s = \{F, T\}$, `piAntidiag {F,T} n` contains functions $k : \text{Bool} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $k(F) + k(T) = n$, corresponding to $(n-j, j)$ for $j = 0, \ldots, n$. The multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{n-j, j} = \binom{n}{j}$ is the standard binomial coefficient. So $P(k) = \binom{n}{j} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}$ — exactly the binomial PMF. This shows `binomial-theorem-oq-03` (binomial distribution) is a special case derivable from this more general formalization.

title: Concrete Sanity Check and the Coordinate Mean
content: `fair_coin_three_flips` is a closed numerical instance: three flips of a $1/2$-coin sum to $1$ over the four outcomes $(3,0),(2,1),(1,2),(0,3)$ with probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$, closed by `norm_num` after expanding the pair sum. The former `rfl` placeholder `multinomial_expectation` (which restated the tautology $\sum_k P(k)\,w(k) = \sum_k P(k)\,w(k)$) has been replaced by `multinomial_mean`, a genuine moment formula: $\sum_k P(k)\,k_i = n\,p_i$, i.e. $E[X_i] = n p_i$.
mathContext: `multinomial_mean` is proved by differentiating the MGF. Specializing the weight $g_j = e^t$ for $j=i$ and $g_j = 1$ otherwise reduces `multinomial_mgf_real` to the one-variable identity $(p_i e^t + (1-p_i))^n = \sum_k P(k)\,e^{t k_i}$ for all $t$; differentiating both sides at $t=0$ and applying uniqueness of the derivative ($\partial_t\,\text{LHS}|_0 = n p_i$, $\partial_t\,\text{RHS}|_0 = \sum_k P(k)\,k_i$) yields $E[X_i] = n p_i$. Differentiating the same identity a *second* time at $t=0$ now also yields the variance $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = n p_i(1-p_i)$ (`multinomial_variance`, via `multinomial_second_moment`); the covariance $\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j) = -n p_i p_j$ for $i\neq j$ remains a follow-up.

title: Second Moment and Variance via the Second MGF Derivative
content: Differentiating the single-coordinate MGF identity $(p_i e^t + (1-p_i))^n = \sum_k P(k)\,e^{t k_i}$ a *second* time at $t=0$ produces the raw second moment. The right-hand side, a finite sum, differentiates termwise to $\sum_k P(k)\,k_i^2\,e^{t k_i}$, which at $t=0$ is $E[X_i^2] = \sum_k P(k)\,k_i^2$. The left-hand side, by the product rule applied to $n\,(p_i e^t+(1-p_i))^{n-1}(p_i e^t)$, evaluates at $t=0$ (where the base is $1$) to $n(n-1)p_i^2 + n p_i = n^2 p_i^2 + n p_i(1-p_i)$. Uniqueness of the derivative equates them (`multinomial_second_moment`). The variance then follows by expanding $\sum_k P(k)(k_i - n p_i)^2$ and substituting the three closed-form sums — normalization, mean, and second moment — giving $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = n p_i(1-p_i)$ (`multinomial_variance`).
mathContext: `multinomial_mgf_exp` packages the shared exponential MGF identity (formerly inlined in `multinomial_mean`). Both derivative computations reuse `HasDerivAt.pow`, `HasDerivAt.mul` (product rule), `HasDerivAt.const_mul`, `HasDerivAt.sum`, `Real.hasDerivAt_exp`, and `HasDerivAt.unique`; the second-derivative coefficient $\uparrow(n-1)$ is reconciled with the real $n-1$ by a case split on $n$. This is the multinomial generalization of the binomial variance $np(1-p)$, exhibiting each coordinate $X_i$ as marginally $\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p_i)$ at the level of its first two moments.

title: multinomial_count: |s|^n = ∑ Multinomial Coefficients
content: `multinomial_count` proves $|s|^n = \sum_{k \in \text{piAntidiag}\, s\, n} \binom{n}{k}$ by applying `sum_pow_eq_sum_piAntidiag` with $f \equiv 1$: $(\sum_{i \in s} 1)^n = (|s|)^n$ and $\prod_{i \in s} 1^{k(i)} = 1$. This is the multinomial analog of $\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j} = 2^n$. For $|s| = 2$: the identity says $2^n = \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}$ (sum of binomial coefficients). The proof uses `simp` with `one_pow`, `prod_const_one`, `sum_const`, and cast lemmas.
mathContext: The identity $|s|^n = \sum_{k} \binom{n}{k}$ counts two things: $|s|^n$ is the number of functions $\text{Fin}\, n \to s$ (all sequences of $n$ choices from $s$); $\sum_k \binom{n}{k}$ counts by distributing $n$ trials into outcome categories. The bijection is: any function $f : \text{Fin}\, n \to s$ induces an outcome count $k(i) = |f^{-1}(\{i\})|$, and $\binom{n}{k}$ counts the functions with that distribution. This is the counting argument underlying both the multinomial theorem and the multinomial distribution.
